w: Wrocław's Gothic town hall has presided over the Market Square since the 13th century, and its cellar claims to be even older in spirit - the Świdnicka Cellar is billed as the oldest restaurant in Europe. Above ground, civic events and concerts; below, beer since medieval merchants ran the square.
s: Home to the oldest restaurant in Europe, allegedly
_facts: Gothic town hall at the centre of Wrocław's Market Square, built from the 13th century
Houses the bourgeois museum and is used for civic and cultural events
Its cellar restaurant, Świdnicka Cellar, is claimed to be the oldest restaurant in Europe

n: St. Vincent and St. James Cathedral
w: This Gothic cathedral in Wrocław's Old Town has buried Polish kings and now serves a very different congregation - it's the seat of the Ukrainian Catholic Eparchy of Wrocław. Centuries of shifting borders and faiths, all under one roof, recognised today as a Historic Monument of Poland alongside the Old Town around it.
s: A Gothic cathedral that buried kings, now a Ukrainian see
_facts: Gothic cathedral in Wrocław's Old Town, seat of the Ukrainian Catholic Eparchy of Wrocław
One of the burial sites of Polish monarchs
Listed as a Historic Monument of Poland alongside the Old Town of Wrocław

w: Kaiser Wilhelm II turned up for the opening of this Oder suspension bridge in 1910, back when it was called the Kaiserbrücke. Renamed twice since - Bridge of Freedom under Weimar, Grunwald Bridge after the war - it survived WWII damage and a 1947 repair, and still carries trams across the river.
s: The Oder bridge a Kaiser opened, renamed twice since
_facts: Suspension bridge over the Oder, built 1908-1910, opened by Emperor Wilhelm II
Originally called the Kaiserbrücke (Imperial Bridge), later the Bridge of Freedom
Built of Silesian granite, 112.5 metres long
Damaged in WWII, repaired and reopened in September 1947; still carries a tram line

w: Planted in 1811 to teach medical students their herbs, Wrocław's botanical garden took collateral damage when Napoleonic-era fortress demolitions wrecked part of the grounds. A filled-in branch of the Oder is now a lily pond, and the garden - Poland's second oldest of its kind - has been protected since 1974.
s: Poland's second-oldest botanical garden, war scars and all
_facts: Founded in 1811 in the Ostrów Tumski area for medical students
Damaged during the Napoleonic Wars when city fortifications were destroyed
Second oldest garden of its type in Poland, after Kraków
A large lily pond now occupies a former filled-in branch of the Oder

w: Couples once sealed their devotion here with padlocks stamped with their names, earning this footbridge its nickname: the Bridge of Lovers. Built in steel in 1889 to replace an older wooden crossing, it links Cathedral Island to Sand Island - a short hop over the Oder that has outlasted plenty of the relationships it locked in.
s: Wrocław's 'Bridge of Lovers', padlocks and all
_facts: Steel footbridge built in 1889, replacing an older wooden bridge
Connects Cathedral Island (Ostrów Tumski) with Sand Island
Pedestrians only; informally known as the Bridge of Lovers, once covered in padlocks

w: Built for a 1913 exhibition marking a century since the German Wars of Liberation, this garden has quietly outlived the empire that built it. Tucked into Szczytnicki Park, it holds close to 270 varieties of trees and shrubs, dozens of them Japanese natives - a slice of Kyoto that Wrocław never gave up.
s: A slice of Japan planted for a long-gone empire's centenary
_facts: Founded 1909-1913 as an exotic garden for the Centennial Exhibition, when Wrocław was the German city of Breslau
Located in Szczytnicki Park near the Centennial Hall
Home to almost 270 taxa of woody plants, including 38 species endemic to Japan

n: Church of Our Lady on the Sand
w: One of Poland's oldest Gothic churches, founded in the 12th century on a spit of land in the Oder, gave its Latin name - Sancta Maria in Arena - to the whole island around it. Sand Island still carries that name today, eight centuries after a handful of monks decided this scrap of river silt was worth building on.
s: The 12th-century church that named an entire island
_facts: Catholic church on Sand Island in the Oder, founded in the 12th century
One of the oldest Gothic churches in Poland
Its Latin name, Sancta Maria in Arena, gave Sand Island its name

w: Built in 1906 with reinforced concrete trusses cutting-edge for Europe at the time, Wrocław's Market Hall was one of two identical halls built to get street traders off the roads. Its twin on Kolejowa Street didn't survive the war; this one did, and after refits in the 1980s and 2010s it's still one of the city's biggest produce markets.
s: A 1900s produce market built with cutting-edge concrete
_facts: Food hall designed by Richard Plüddemann, built 1906-1908 as the Breslauer Markthalle Nr 1
Innovative use of reinforced concrete trusses, unique in Europe at the time
Its twin hall on Kolejowa Street was destroyed in WWII and demolished in 1973
Refurbished in 1980-83 and 2018-19; still one of the city's biggest produce markets

w: Once a residence of the Prussian monarchy, the Royal Palace at the heart of Wrocław has since traded its crown for display cases. It's now home to the city museum, the grandest address in town given over to telling Wrocław's own story - kings and commoners under the same roof at last.
s: A former royal palace, now the city's museum
_facts: Originally a palace of the Prussian monarchy
Now houses the Wrocław city museum

w: Completed in 1872, the New Synagogue was once one of the largest in the German Empire and the beating heart of Reform Judaism in Breslau - until the Kristallnacht pogrom burned it down on 9 November 1938. Nothing remains of the building, but the name still marks the spot.
s: The Reform synagogue burned down on Kristallnacht
_facts: Reform Jewish congregation and synagogue, designed by Edwin Oppler in Romanesque Revival style, completed 1872
One of the largest synagogues in the German Empire and a centre of Reform Judaism in Breslau
Destroyed during the Kristallnacht pogrom of 9-10 November 1938

w: Built in 1909 as Breslau's biggest stage - 1,736 seats of operetta and musical theatre - the building survived WWII damage only to reopen in 1950 with a socialist propaganda play about workers rebuilding bombed cities. Gutted by fire again in 1994, this is a theatre that has had to rebuild itself more than once.
s: The theatre that has literally had to rebuild itself twice
_facts: Main building designed by Berlin architect Walter Hentschel, completed 1909
Biggest stage in Wrocław in the early 1930s with 1,736 seats, mostly used for operetta
Damaged at the end of WWII, reconstructed and reopened in 1950
Badly damaged by fire on 18 January 1994

w: German troops wired this bridge with explosives during the 1945 siege of Festung Breslau, braced for an attack that never came from that side - the Red Army struck from the south instead, and the bridge survived. Rebuilt in steel in the 1890s with four Art Nouveau obelisks, it still crosses the Oder by the zoo.
s: The bridge Wehrmacht troops wired to blow, and never did
_facts: Steel truss bridge over the Oder, rebuilt 1895-97 by Karl Klimm under city architect Richard Plüddemann
Features four decorative Art Nouveau obelisks in red sandstone
German soldiers planted explosives to destroy it during the 1945 siege of Festung Breslau, but the Red Army's attack from the south spared it

n: Collegiate Church of the Holy Cross and St. Bartholomew
w: A two-storey Gothic church stacked one sanctuary atop another, this collegiate church on Cathedral Island ranks as Wrocław's second most important Catholic building - and, like its grander neighbour, holds Polish monarchs buried within its walls. A Historic Monument of Poland on the city's oldest island.
s: A two-storey Gothic church built one floor atop another
_facts: Two-storey brick Gothic collegiate church on Ostrów Tumski (Cathedral Island)
Considered the second most important Roman Catholic church in Wrocław
One of the historic burial sites of Polish monarchs
Listed as a Historic Monument of Poland alongside the Old Town of Wrocław
